blocks.text: Stomata (singular = stoma) are the tiny openings or pores present within the plant tissues which are necessary for gaseous exchange. These are typically found in leaves but can even be present in some stems. The stomata are surrounded by specialized cells or the guard cells that facilitate the opening and closing of the stomatal pores. Guard cells are bean-shaped and contain chloroplasts. Guard cells can open and close depending on environmental conditions. The opening and closing of stomata control the transpiration rate in plants.

blocks.alt: A surface view of leaf epidermis, a pavement of wavy-edged cells. On the left an open stoma: two bean-shaped guard cells bowed apart around a dark lens-shaped pore. On the right a closed stoma: the two guard cells straight and pressed together so the pore is only a thin line. Labels: Guard cell, Pore, Open stoma, Closed stoma.
blocks.caption: Figure 8.4: Scanning electron micrograph (SEM) of open and closed stomata on a lavender leaf (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 8.4).

blocks.text: During daylight, stomata open to allow CO₂ to enter the plant for photosynthesis. The opening of stomata is primarily regulated by guard cells. At night, when photosynthesis ceases due to lack of light, stomata typically close to conserve water. However, plants still respire, taking in O₂ and releasing CO₂. The closure of stomata at night helps minimize water loss through transpiration.
